questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
Over the past 4-5 years I have developed a personal and academic interest in Korean history, language and culture. Knowing that my master's thesis would be related to Korean history in some way was a serious academic motivator to choose South Korea. Just as importantly, though, I also wanted to experience the culture and society myself before fully settling on a direction for my thesis.
I also wanted to go far away from home now that I had the chance to do so with the backing of UCPH and for an extended period of time. I wanted to push myself out of my comfort zone.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer:
That depends on the kind of information. Generally, the information I received was very, very good until I arrived. After that, I didn't receive a lot and usually pretty late from both the university and immigration. Orientation was cancelled, instead we received a PDF with relevant information, which was pretty useful even though I think a physical orientation would have been better. 
I got most of my information from the chat for international students in the SNU Buddy Programme.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I joined the SNU Buddy Programme and was assigned a personal buddy to help me when needed. I didn't reach out for help, but I know that others did and was very happy with it. I didn't personally reach out to the International Admissions Office either, but heard from others that due to a change in staff the level of help had dropped pretty significantly.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
I think it depends on personal priorities. I found it pretty difficult, because I wanted to live with other students. There are a few facebook groups for exchange students in Seoul that I looked at and there were many offers, but I don't know how legit they were. I ended up getting a bed at a shared apartment run by SNU alumni, but it was pretty far away from campus. I loved the neighborhood that I ended up in, but it was very impractical when I went to class or wanted to join social events. I found the sharehouse through SNU's website on a page for off campus housing.
Living in a sharehouse is pretty great, though, because there will probably be international students living there who have already been there a semester or more and can guide you through the process of immigration registration and so on.
Other students who lived off campus lived in so called goshiwon, which are tiny private rooms with a shared common areas, usually run by older ladies who provide basic food such as rice and noodles covered by the rent. Some used these as temporary housing until they found something better. Other students rented on airbnb.
One recommendation is to sign a short term contract at first if possible or make sure you can get out of it quickly, since I was offered a room at the dorms two weeks into the semester. Since I hadn't expected this and had signed a contract for my entire stay I decided to stay in my sharehouse.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
It definitely gives you a different exchange experience from the people living in the dorms. The dorms don't really have kitchens, so if you live off campus you'll have the option to cook for yourself, while you'll automatically try a lot of restaurants if you're at the dorms. 
SNU's campus is pretty isolated and far away from the center of the city, so living off campus gives you a lot more options to be closer to the interesting things - then you'll have to factor in transportation to campus, though, but the public transport system in Seoul is very, very good and affordable. The only issue is the bus to the campus from the subway station. It is always packed and there's an extremely long queue to get on it, so you'll have to wait for up to an hour. Apparently the shuttle is better, and you can also walk if you're up for it and have time.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It wasn't easy, but it was far from impossible

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
There are multiple stages of class registration at SNU.
In the first stage you choose the courses that you find interesting and put them in you basket. You can then see a time table of a week of these classes so you can plan them without overlaps, their number of credits and a syllabus. I think I could choose up to 9 courses of interest and you can see how many other students have placed it in their basket to get a feel of there popularity.
A few days later in the next stage you will choose the courses you register for. This is first come, first serve, and once the amount of students allowed has been reached it closes for registration. 
If you didn't get to register for a course that you wanted you would have the option of contacting the professor teaching the course directly and ask for permission to register as an additional student.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: There was a trial run of the stages a week before the real thing and a guide was sent to us. It was a bit difficult to figure out and seemed to assume that you had a bit of previous experience or inside knowledge, but it made a lot more sense once I got access to the website.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got the courses that I wanted.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
I have a couple pieces of advice:
First, make sure to try the trial run before the actual registration if you have any doubts on the process. I misunderstood the dates and didn't join the trial run in time, so I had to figure it out in the actual registration. It worked out well, but I would have liked to have tried it out first.
Second, you have a bit of flexibility in the amount of credits you're allowed to take each semester. You can register for more courses than you actually need and drop one that you might not like within the first month of the semester. I joined a course that ended up being very, very different from the course description, so some of them have to be tried out before you really know what they're about.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
I had three courses. One was a basic history course providing a presentation of modern Korean history. It was very simple since it was probably meant as an introduction for international students to Korean society.
My two other courses were more "real" in the sense that they had a more even split between international and local students. The level was high, but not very different from at home in Copenhagen.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Pretty similar to what I'm used to at UCPH. Most classes started with a lecture from the teacher/professor which was followed up by a student presentation and a class discussion.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Modern Korean History and Society
Case Studies on Transnational Issues and International Cooperation
European Integration

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Modern Korean History and Society seems to be a course that is provided most if not all semesters and it gives you a good introduction to the history of Korea since the late 1800s and the fall of the Joseon Dynasty in early 1900s and until recent time. 
I don't know if the other courses will be provided again, but the teacher of Transnational Issues and International Cooperation (dr. Lee JaeWon) was very, very good and is going to continue teaching as an external lecturer at SNU.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: My plane ticket home was cancelled and I had to buy a new one that was almost twice as expensive as first planned

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Certain groceries such as dairy products and vegetables/fruits were more expensive than expected.
Insurance ended up being more expensive than I had expected.
The cost of rent at the dorms was much lower than what I ended up paying at my sharehouse.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Apparently there were quite a lot, but since I lived far away from campus I didn't participate in any.
I was a member of the SNU Buddy programme, but I had very mixed experiences with it.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I heard positive things about the taekwondo club. 
If you know you'll want and be able to participate, the SNU Buddy programme will be very good.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Just experience the city. I had planned a lot of the typical sight seeing-things, but I didn't get to do most of them. 
The café culture in South Korea is absolutely insane and I got to see a lot of the city by finding cafés all around to try. 
I lived in the area of the city called Seongsu and this neighborhood has been an up-and-coming place for a while now and was very, very popular. It's known for cafés and pop up-stores.
People interested in history would probably want to see at least on of the palaces or keep an eye out for news on parades.
There are constantly festivals to join.
Fans of K-pop should keep an eye out for exhibitions for there favorite groups and I think most should try to go a concert to experience it.
I also think it's very important to go outside of Seoul at least once. I went to the South Jeolla Province and it was great to experience a different part of Korea both in terms of nature and culture. It's very easy to be overwhelmed by the stress of Seoul, but other cities are much more calm. I didn't get to go myself, but if I could go again, I would go to Busan for a few days.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer:
Sometimes it was easy, sometimes it was difficult. I think I know enough about Korean culture to be able to navigate in most situations, but 
I don't think I adjusted in the time that I was there. Being very obviously non-Korean, it's difficult to go anywhere without drawing some kind of attention. You have to get used to being stared at on the train and strangers asking you where you're from. Most of the time it's fine and people are very nice.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer:
At SNU specifically, the local students are overall pretty good at English, so there's not much of a language barrier. There is also a requirement that all students must take at least one course in English, so exchange students will probably have classes with a lot of local students. If you're comfortable socializing it should be pretty simple to make connections with the local Korean students. 
The SNU Buddy programme also provided a lot of contact with local students.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer:
I don't think it was anything on the side of the Korean locals, but I personally felt hyperaware of Danish people's reputation of being very informal. I think I maybe overcompensated by becoming too polite and reserved at times.
Also, when you're out in shops (supermarkets, clothing stores, make up stores, etc.) the staff will follow you around in case you need help. Sometimes they'll be silent, sometimes they'll make suggestions. It made me feel very uncomfortable and avoid shops altogether for a little while.
If you don't look Korean, you will be stared at and potentially commented on. Sometimes people will come up to you and ask where you're from or random questions.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer:
Something is always happening. You'll run into a filming set and crew, a celebrity event, a pop-up store, a temporary exhibition and/or a festival pretty much everywhere you go all the time. 
The mix between the extremely modern and the very traditional and historic is pretty amazing.
It's definitely a culture of contrasts. You'll see a Porsche drive past a row of run down buildings, people dressed their absolute best and people in hoodies and curlers in their bangs, quick convenience store food and themed, over-the-top cafés.
People are (generally) very expressive and enthusiastic which is really great to see.
The food is amazing and I was never disappointed in anything I got.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
SNU is the most prestigious university in South Korea. Everyone you tell that you are a student there will respond with "Korea number 1!" or "You must be very smart!". It's easy to expect the academic level and expectations to be impossibly high, but really it's all very reasonable. A level of politeness and formality is of course expected, but it's not extreme. Communication from the university is not great. 
The language course is apparently very good, but I think this is true especially if you have no previous experience with the language and need help to learn it while you're in Seoul. I had learned a bit before going and didn't take the language course and I pretty quickly learned to order at cafés and restaurants in Korean. Also, people in service jobs are generally able to speak English in Seoul. But download the app Papago, it's the best translator and I used it daily.
The SNU campus in on a mountain side. Be prepared to walk on hills a lot.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: I can't think of more.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: I've confirmed my interest in Korea and its language, culture and history, and I've learned a lot about myself, what I want to do in the future and become a lot stronger from the experience.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer:
Even when I was with people or called home I would feel very alone. The other students that I spoke to said they felt the same thing. People back home keep living their own lives and even if you become really close with the people you meet, they still only know you in the context of exchange. It's a very overwhelming experience that is mainly understood by other people who have gone through something similar. 
In terms of practical difficulties, getting the registration number and card is definitely a process and I wasn't prepared for it, so I think students going to South Korea should be aware of it and the process before arriving.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: South Korea is a great place to go and not just for people with a prior interest in the country or culture.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
